problem: The answer text is broken: it reads "For f  0, H(f) = −j, so the spectrum is X(f) + X(f) = 2X(f)". The comparison signs are lost, and the negative-frequency half of the argument — the part that actually explains why negative frequencies cancel — is missing. A student copying this learns only half the reason and cannot see why the negative side vanishes.
fix: For f < 0, H(f) = +j, so j·H(f)·X(f) = j(j)X(f) = −X(f); the spectrum is X(f) − X(f) = 0. For f > 0, H(f) = −j, so j·H(f)·X(f) = j(−j)X(f) = +X(f); the spectrum is X(f) + X(f) = 2X(f). Negative frequencies cancel, positive frequencies double.

problem: The symbol h̃(t) is defined only as "the low-pass equivalent impulse response". The chapter never states how h̃ relates to the real band-pass impulse response h(t), so the factor 1/2 in the formula cannot be checked by the reader.
fix: Add: h(t) = Re{h̃(t)e^(j2πfc t)}, that is, h̃(t) is the complex envelope of h(t). Then y(t) = Re{ỹ(t)e^(j2πfc t)} with ỹ = (1/2) x̃ * h̃.

problem: "Real band-pass signals have matching positive and negative frequencies" is vague; the technical property that makes the Hilbert transform work is conjugate symmetry of the spectrum.
fix: Real signals have a conjugate-symmetric spectrum, X(−f) = X*(f), so the negative-frequency half carries no new information and the positive half alone can describe the signal.
